title: The margin of appreciation and judicial deference
subtitle: Two dials, one instinct: when courts step back from a moral or political question
objectives: Distinguish the margin of appreciation (an international-law doctrine restraining Strasbourg) from domestic judicial deference (a separate, UK-court restraint on itself)
State the 'mirror principle' from Ullah and explain why and how the UK courts retreated from it
Identify the institutional reasons UK courts give for deferring to Parliament or the executive in politically or morally contested cases, and apply that reasoning to a new fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.role: Founding statement of the margin of appreciation: Strasbourg defers to the state's own assessment of local moral and social conditions
The 'mirror principle' — domestic courts should go no further, and no less far, than Strasbourg's own case law

leadingAuthorities.citation: R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice [2014] UKSC 38
leadingAuthorities.role: Domestic deference to Parliament on a morally contested question, even where the court has jurisdiction to rule

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often reach for 'the margin of appreciation' to explain any UK court declining to intervene — including in purely domestic cases where Strasbourg is nowhere in the room. Where the profile shows this conflation, this note appears: 'You know both doctrines exist — this lesson is about which dial you're actually looking at.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can define both doctrines accurately. The test pool below leans on fact patterns that require you to say which dial is moving and why — margin of appreciation and domestic deference are easy to blur under exam pressure.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and hold the two dials apart before anything else: one belongs to Strasbourg, one belongs to the UK courts. Nothing later in this lesson makes sense if those two get merged.

overview.hook: Picture two dials, not one. The first belongs to Strasbourg, and it turns depending on how much room a member state gets to run its own affairs before the European Court of Human Rights will call foul. The second belongs to the UK's own courts, and it turns depending on how much room Parliament and the executive get before a domestic judge will step in. Confuse the two dials — as students very often do — and you'll misdescribe what's actually happening in cases from obscenity law to assisted dying.

parts.heading: Dial one: the margin of appreciation is Strasbourg's, not ours
parts.voice: spectrum — introduces the dial metaphor and locates it precisely
body: Start with what the margin of appreciation actually is: a doctrine of international law, applied by the European Court of Human Rights when it reviews a complaint against a member state. It is not a doctrine the UK Supreme Court applies to itself. That single sentence resolves a surprising share of exam confusion.

The doctrine's logic is one of institutional humility at the international level. Forty-six states with different histories, moral traditions and social conditions have all signed the Convention. Strasbourg accepts that on genuinely contested questions — public morals, national security, the boundaries of family life — a domestic authority is often better placed than an international court sitting in France to judge what its own society needs. The margin is the space Strasbourg leaves for that local judgment before it will find a violation.

Crucially, the margin is not fixed. It widens on questions Strasbourg treats as genuinely contested across Europe (there being no European consensus, say, on gambling advertising) and narrows sharply on questions where a consensus exists or where a right is close to absolute. Learn it as a dial, not a switch: wide margin, light-touch review; narrow margin, close review.

components.definition: The latitude the European Court of Human Rights allows a Contracting State in deciding how to meet its Convention obligations, reflecting that national authorities are, in principle, better placed than an international court to assess local conditions and needs — an international-law doctrine, applied by Strasbourg to states, not by UK courts to themselves.

components.factsShort: A publisher was convicted under UK obscenity law for distributing a schoolbook considered too explicit for children. He argued this breached his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.
components.ratioShort: Because there is no uniform European conception of 'morals', the state is best placed to judge what its own public morals require, and Strasbourg will only intervene where a state's assessment is clearly unreasonable.

expanded.facts: Handyside published 'The Little Red Schoolbook', an educational text aimed at schoolchildren that included frank sections on sex. UK authorities seized and destroyed copies and secured his conviction under the Obscene Publications Act. He complained to Strasbourg that this violated his Article 10 right to freedom of expression.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court held that Article 10(2) leaves to Contracting States a margin of appreciation, because state authorities are, by reason of their direct and continuous contact with the vital forces of their countries, in a better position than the international judge to give an opinion on the exact content of requirements of morals as well as on the necessity of a restriction intended to meet them.
expanded.significance: This is the doctrine's founding statement. It is worth memorising as a formula: no uniform European morality, direct contact with local conditions, better placed than an international judge. Every later margin-of-appreciation case is a variation on this reasoning.

interaction.prompt: The margin of appreciation is applied by which court, to whom?
options: The European Court of Human Rights, to Contracting States
The UK Supreme Court, to Parliament and the executive
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Keep this pinned down before anything else in this lesson: the margin of appreciation is Strasbourg's restraint on itself when reviewing a state, not a UK court's restraint on itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — that description belongs to domestic deference, which is a separate doctrine covered later in this lesson. The margin of appreciation is specifically Strasbourg's restraint when it reviews a Contracting State's own conduct.

parts.heading: The mirror principle — and why it couldn't hold
parts.voice: spectrum — tracks the dial's setting from fixed to variable
body: When the Human Rights Act brought Convention rights into UK law, a hard question followed immediately: how closely should UK courts track Strasbourg's own case law? Section 2 HRA says only that domestic courts must 'take into account' Strasbourg jurisprudence — a deliberately loose instruction. The House of Lords in Ullah turned it into something much tighter.

Lord Bingham's formula in Ullah became known as the mirror principle: a national court should not, without strong reason, dilute or diminish a Convention right as interpreted by Strasbourg — but nor, and this is the less-quoted half, should it go further than Strasbourg's own case law requires. 'No more, but certainly no less.' For a period, UK courts largely tracked Strasbourg's settled position as a ceiling and a floor at once.

The mirror principle didn't survive intact. UK courts — most visibly in the Supreme Court's approach to hearsay evidence, and repeatedly since — pushed back on the idea that domestic courts must always wait for Strasbourg to move first, especially where UK common law and constitutional tradition already spoke clearly to an issue. The modern position is a genuine dialogue: UK courts give Strasbourg case law considerable weight, but treat themselves as free to decline to follow a Strasbourg decision that sits uneasily with domestic constitutional principle, particularly where Strasbourg itself has not spoken with a single clear voice.

Watch the dial move here: Ullah sets it to something close to 'follow precisely'; the retreat since sets it to 'weigh seriously, but reserve the right to differ'. That shift is itself a form of institutional confidence — UK courts becoming more willing to reason to their own answer rather than deferring reflexively to an international court.

components.definition: Lord Bingham's formula from Ullah: a domestic court interpreting a Convention right should keep pace with Strasbourg's own jurisprudence — no more, but certainly no less — a position since qualified rather than abandoned outright.

interaction.prompt: Where does the modern UK courts' relationship with Strasbourg case law sit — closer to 'must follow precisely' (the strict Ullah mirror) or 'weigh seriously, but may reason to a different answer'?
interaction.explanation: The strict mirror principle from Ullah has been qualified by later domestic case law: UK courts give Strasbourg jurisprudence real weight but no longer treat themselves as bound to track it exactly, particularly where Strasbourg has not spoken clearly or where domestic constitutional tradition points a different way.

parts.heading: Dial two: domestic deference, and why it isn't the same dial
parts.voice: spectrum — introduces the second, distinct dial and its institutional logic
body: Now the second dial. Domestic deference is not about Strasbourg at all — it describes UK courts choosing to give weight to Parliament's or the executive's own judgment on a question, even where the court plainly has jurisdiction to decide the case itself. The vocabulary sometimes borrows 'margin' language loosely, but the justification is entirely domestic: separation of powers, institutional competence, and democratic legitimacy.

The reasoning recurs in a recognisable pattern. Elected, accountable Parliament — not an unelected court — is said to be the more legitimate forum for resolving questions with no single legally correct answer: how to balance national security against liberty, how to weigh competing moral views in society, how to allocate scarce public resources. Courts are also said to be institutionally less well equipped than Parliament to gather evidence, hear a full range of competing interests, and revisit a settled rule through ordinary democratic and legislative processes rather than a single binary judgment on the facts of one case.

National security is the paradigm example students reach for first, and it is a genuine one: courts have repeatedly said that assessments of what measures a threat actually requires call for expertise and information the executive holds and the judiciary does not. But treat that as one instance of the reasoning, not the whole of it — the same institutional logic surfaces just as often on morally contested social questions that have nothing to do with security at all, as the next part of this lesson shows.

components.label: Why UK courts say they defer
points: Democratic legitimacy — Parliament is elected and accountable; courts are not
Institutional competence — Parliament can hear wider evidence and a fuller range of interests than a single case allows
Reversibility — a legislative rule can be revisited and changed; a single court ruling settles only the case in front of it
Subject-matter expertise — on national security or complex policy trade-offs, the executive often holds information and expertise courts do not

interaction.prompt: Which of the following best captures why UK courts defer to Parliament on some human rights questions?
options: Because the margin of appreciation, as a rule of Strasbourg law, is binding on UK courts too

Because institutional factors — democratic legitimacy, evidence-gathering capacity, reversibility — make Parliament a more legitimate forum for some contested questions, even where the court has jurisdiction to decide
Because Parliament's decisions on human rights questions cannot be reviewed by any UK court
interaction.trapExplanation: The first option is the exact conflation this lesson exists to prevent: the margin of appreciation binds Strasbourg's own review of states, not UK courts reviewing UK law. The third overstates the position — UK courts retain jurisdiction and can and do rule against Parliament; deference is a reason to give weight to Parliament's judgment, not a jurisdictional bar.

parts.heading: Nicklinson: a court that could rule, and chose restraint
parts.voice: spectrum — slows down; states the legal reasoning with care before any doctrinal takeaway
body: Tony Nicklinson suffered a catastrophic stroke in 2005 that left him with locked-in syndrome: fully mentally alert, but almost entirely unable to move or speak, able to communicate only through small movements of his eyes and head. He described his life afterwards as one of unbearable indignity and wished to end it, but his paralysis meant he could not do so without assistance — assistance that section 2 of the Suicide Act 1961 makes a criminal offence to provide. He brought a claim, later continued by his widow after his death and joined by another claimant, Paul Lamb, arguing that the blanket criminal ban was incompatible with his right to respect for private life under Article 8.

This lesson is not the place to argue the rights and wrongs of assisted dying, and it deliberately doesn't try to. What it is the place to examine closely is the Supreme Court's legal reasoning about who should decide. A majority of the Court held that it did have the constitutional authority to consider whether the blanket ban was compatible with Article 8, and to grant a declaration of incompatibility if it concluded it was not. Having established that it could act, a majority nonetheless declined to make that declaration on this occasion — holding that Parliament, not the courts, was the more appropriate body to resolve a question with such profound and contested ethical, social and religious dimensions, particularly since Parliament had recently considered and rejected changes to the law itself.

Notice exactly what kind of deference this is. It is not Strasbourg's margin of appreciation — no international court is involved. It is not a claim that courts lack jurisdiction — the majority expressly held that they had it. It is a reasoned, and contestable, judgment that on a question this morally divisive, with no single legally compelled answer, the institution best placed to weigh competing views and decide whether and how to change the law is an elected Parliament that can hear the full range of medical, ethical and social evidence — not a court bound to the facts of one claimant's case.

That is the exact shape of domestic deference this lesson has been building towards: a court with the power to rule choosing institutional restraint, and giving reasons for that restraint that are about competence and legitimacy, not about doubt over its own authority to act.

components.factsShort: Tony Nicklinson, who had locked-in syndrome following a catastrophic stroke, challenged the blanket criminal prohibition on assisted suicide as incompatible with his Article 8 right to respect for private life.
components.ratioShort: The Supreme Court has the constitutional authority to rule on the Article 8 compatibility of the assisted suicide ban and to grant a declaration of incompatibility, but a majority declined to do so, holding that Parliament was institutionally better placed to resolve a question this ethically contested.

expanded.facts: Nicklinson was almost completely paralysed and unable to speak following a stroke, though mentally unimpaired. He wished to end his life but could not do so unaided, and assisting him would have been a criminal offence under s 2 of the Suicide Act 1961. He sought a declaration that the blanket ban was incompatible with Article 8. He died shortly after his claim was rejected at first instance; his widow continued the litigation, joined by Paul Lamb, who had a different but similarly severe condition.
expanded.judgmentExtract: A majority of the nine-Justice panel held that the Supreme Court had the constitutional authority to make a declaration that s 2 was incompatible with Article 8, rejecting the argument that this question was categorically beyond the judicial role. However, a majority (differently composed) also concluded that it should not exercise that power on the facts of this case, given the recency and closeness of Parliament's own consideration of the issue, and the institutional advantages Parliament held in assessing the wider ethical, medical and social evidence involved.
expanded.significance: Nicklinson is taught as the clearest modern illustration of domestic deference operating independently of jurisdictional doubt: the Court affirmed its own authority to rule and still chose restraint, on reasoned institutional grounds. It is regularly cited alongside national security cases to show that deference is not confined to matters of state security — it extends to any question a court judges to be more legitimately resolved through the democratic process.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that captures why the Supreme Court declined to grant a declaration of incompatibility in Nicklinson, despite holding that it had the power to do so.
interaction.passage: The Court held that it had jurisdiction to determine whether section 2 of the Suicide Act 1961 was compatible with Article 8, and that this was not a question categorically beyond the judicial role. Having established that authority, a majority nonetheless concluded that Parliament, having recently and closely considered reform of this area and being better placed to weigh the full range of ethical, medical and social evidence, was the more appropriate body to decide whether and how the law should change. The claim for a declaration of incompatibility was accordingly dismissed.
interaction.ratioSentence: Having established that authority, a majority nonetheless concluded that Parliament, having recently and closely considered reform of this area and being better placed to weigh the full range of ethical, medical and social evidence, was the more appropriate body to decide whether and how the law should change.

parts.heading: Reading the dial: what moves it, and what doesn't
parts.voice: spectrum — closes by teaching the dial as a transferable diagnostic skill
body: Bring both dials together and you have a genuinely useful exam tool. First ask: is Strasbourg involved at all? If the question concerns an application to the European Court of Human Rights against the UK, you're on dial one — the margin of appreciation, and you should be asking how contested the subject matter is across Contracting States. If the question concerns a UK court reviewing UK law or executive action, you're on dial two — domestic deference — and Strasbourg's margin is, at most, background context, not the operative doctrine.

Second, within dial two, ask what is actually moving the setting. National security cases push the dial towards deference because courts say they lack the expertise and information Parliament and the executive hold. Nicklinson-style cases push the dial towards deference for a different reason: not a lack of information, but a judgment that the question is one of contested political morality without a single legally correct answer, which an elected body is better placed to resolve. Both produce restraint; the reasons are not identical, and a strong answer names which one is doing the work on the facts in front of you.

Third, remember the dial can also swing the other way. Courts defer less — sometimes not at all — on questions closer to the core of a right, where an answer is legally determinate, or where fundamental fair-trial or non-discrimination guarantees are engaged. Deference is a reasoned choice made case by case, not a constitutional off-switch that Parliament or the executive can simply invoke.

components.title: Which dial is moving?
components.description: A diagnostic flowchart distinguishing the margin of appreciation from domestic judicial deference, and identifying what is driving deference within a domestic case.

nodes.label: Is the European Court of Human Rights reviewing the UK's compliance with the Convention?
Yes → dial one: margin of appreciation — ask how much European consensus exists on the issue
No, a UK court is reviewing UK law/executive action → dial two: domestic deference
Is the reason for restraint a lack of expertise/information the executive holds (e.g. national security)?
Or is it that the question is one of contested political/social morality without a single legally correct answer (e.g. Nicklinson)?
Does the case instead concern the core of a right, or a legally determinate question? → expect less deference, closer review

components.textAlternative: First ask whether Strasbourg itself is reviewing the UK's compliance with the Convention — if so, you are on the margin of appreciation, and the key question is how much consensus exists across Contracting States on the issue. If instead a UK court is reviewing UK law or executive action, you are on domestic deference. Within that, ask what is driving any restraint: a lack of expertise or information the executive holds (as in national security cases), or a judgment that the question is one of contested political or social morality without a single legally correct answer (as in Nicklinson). Where a case instead concerns the core of a right or a legally determinate question, expect less deference and closer judicial review.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is a UK court more likely to give weight to a Nicklinson-style 'Parliament is the more legitimate forum' form of deference, rather than a Handyside-style margin of appreciation or a national-security-style deference to executive expertise?
interaction.scenarioA: A claimant argues that a UK statute banning a controversial medical procedure breaches Article 8, and the case turns on whether Parliament or the courts should resolve a genuinely contested ethical debate with no single correct legal answer, on which Parliament has recently legislated after full debate.
interaction.scenarioB: A claimant challenges a Home Secretary's assessment that a named individual poses a specific security threat, arguing the assessment relied on intelligence the claimant cannot see.
interaction.explanation: Scenario A mirrors Nicklinson precisely: a domestically contested moral question, already the subject of recent parliamentary debate, where the institutional argument for restraint rests on democratic legitimacy rather than a gap in judicial expertise. Scenario B is the national-security paradigm — deference there rests on the executive holding specialist information and expertise the court does not, a different (though related) justification.

testPool.prompt: Define the margin of appreciation and state which court applies it.
acceptableAnswers: space the ECtHR allows a Contracting State to assess local conditions
testPool.modelAnswer: The margin of appreciation is the latitude the European Court of Human Rights allows a Contracting State in deciding how to meet its Convention obligations, reflecting that national authorities are generally better placed than an international court to judge local moral and social conditions.

testPool.prompt: Which case is the founding statement of the margin of appreciation doctrine?
options: Handyside v UK
R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice

testPool.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes the margin of appreciation from domestic judicial deference?
options: They are the same doctrine under two names
The margin of appreciation is Strasbourg's restraint on itself when reviewing states; domestic deference is a UK court's own choice to give weight to Parliament or the executive
The margin of appreciation applies only to Article 8, while domestic deference applies to all Convention rights
testPool.trapExplanation: Students frequently answer as if the two doctrines were interchangeable, or invent an article-specific boundary that doesn't exist. The real distinction is institutional: which court is restraining itself, and towards whom.

testPool.prompt: Name the case that established the 'mirror principle' governing how closely UK courts should track Strasbourg case law.
testPool.modelAnswer: R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator [2004] UKHL 26, in which Lord Bingham held that a domestic court should keep pace with Strasbourg jurisprudence — no more, but certainly no less.

testPool.prompt: Section 2 of the Human Rights Act 1998 requires a UK court to 'take into account' Strasbourg jurisprudence when determining a Convention question. What does the Ullah mirror principle add to this bare statutory instruction?
options: It converts 'take into account' into a rule that courts should not diminish, and should not go further than, a right as Strasbourg has interpreted it — a much tighter instruction than the statute's own wording
It confirms that Strasbourg jurisprudence is legally binding on UK courts in the same way as UK statute
It disapplies section 2 entirely in favour of a purely domestic standard

testPool.prompt: Put these in the order they occurred in the development of the relationship between UK courts and Strasbourg case law.
items: Strasbourg establishes the margin of appreciation as a doctrine restraining its own review of states (Handyside)
The Human Rights Act requires UK courts to 'take into account' Strasbourg jurisprudence
The House of Lords adopts the strict mirror principle in Ullah
UK courts begin to qualify the mirror principle, treating Strasbourg case law as weighty but not strictly binding

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence stating the mirror principle itself.
testPool.passage: The House of Lords considered how closely a domestic court should track the jurisprudence of the Strasbourg court when applying Convention rights under the Human Rights Act. Lord Bingham held that the duty of national courts is to keep pace with the Strasbourg jurisprudence as it evolves over time: no more, but certainly no less. This did not mean a domestic court was barred from ever reaching its own view, but it set the default posture UK courts would adopt for the following decade.
testPool.ratioSentence: Lord Bingham held that the duty of national courts is to keep pace with the Strasbourg jurisprudence as it evolves over time: no more, but certainly no less.

testPool.prompt: On a question where there is a strong, settled consensus across Contracting States (for example, a core fair-trial guarantee), how wide is the margin of appreciation Strasbourg is likely to allow?
testPool.explanation: The margin of appreciation narrows as European consensus grows and as a right moves closer to its core protections; it widens where states genuinely diverge on contested social or moral questions, as in Handyside.

testPool.prompt: A UK court is asked to review a government minister's assessment that a specific piece of intelligence justifies restricting a named individual's freedom of movement on national security grounds. The claimant argues the court should scrutinise the assessment itself in full detail. What is the most likely outcome, and why?
options: The court will likely give the executive's assessment significant weight, reasoning that it lacks the specialist expertise and access to sensitive intelligence that the executive holds
The court will refuse jurisdiction entirely, since national security questions cannot be reviewed under the Human Rights Act
The court will apply the margin of appreciation directly, since this is a Strasbourg-style doctrine available to any UK court
testPool.explanation: This is the paradigm domestic-deference scenario: the UK court retains jurisdiction (ruling out option 2), but is likely to defer significantly to the executive's specialist assessment (not apply Strasbourg's own margin of appreciation, which belongs to a different court reviewing a different question).

testPool.prompt: A claimant argues that a UK court should defer to Parliament's recent, closely contested vote on a controversial social reform bill when deciding whether a related statute is compatible with a qualified Convention right. Which authority most directly supports this argument for deference?
options: R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice
Handyside v UK
R (Ullah) v Special Adjudicator
testPool.explanation: Nicklinson is the leading domestic authority for deferring to Parliament specifically because it has recently and closely considered a morally contested question — a different justification from Handyside's Strasbourg-facing margin or Ullah's mirror-principle concern with tracking Strasbourg case law.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this account of Nicklinson's reasoning that shows the Supreme Court was not doubting its own jurisdiction to rule.
testPool.scenarioText: A majority of the Supreme Court held that it had the constitutional authority to determine whether the blanket ban on assisted suicide was compatible with Article 8. Having established that authority, a majority nonetheless concluded that Parliament was the more appropriate body to decide whether and how the law should change, given its recent and close consideration of the issue.
tappableSpans: held that it had the constitutional authority to determine whether the blanket ban on assisted suicide was compatible with Article 8
Parliament was the more appropriate body to decide whether and how the law should change
given its recent and close consideration of the issue
testPool.correctSpan: held that it had the constitutional authority to determine whether the blanket ban on assisted suicide was compatible with Article 8
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is the fact students most often miss: the Court's restraint was a reasoned institutional choice, not an admission that it lacked the power to act.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that shows the Court affirmed, rather than doubted, its own authority to rule. Everything after that point is about how the Court chose to exercise a power it had already confirmed it held.

testPool.prompt: A campaign group challenges a new UK statute that bans a controversial form of genetic research on Article 8 grounds, arguing the ban serves no rational purpose. Parliament debated and voted on the ban eighteen months ago after an extensive public consultation, and no fresh scientific evidence has emerged since. Using the reasoning in Nicklinson, analyse whether a court is likely to defer to Parliament's judgment on this question.
factsToOrder: The subject matter is scientifically and ethically contested, with no single legally correct answer
Parliament has recently and closely considered the issue, including an extensive public consultation
No fresh evidence has emerged since Parliament's decision
The claimant asks the court to substitute its own judgment on a contested question of policy

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a court should defer to Parliament's judgment in assessing the Article 8 compatibility of the research ban, rather than substituting its own assessment.
modelAnswer.rule: Following Nicklinson, a court with jurisdiction to determine a Convention question may nonetheless decline to displace Parliament's judgment where the question is one of genuinely contested ethical or scientific policy without a single legally correct answer, and where Parliament has recently and closely considered the issue through a full democratic process.
modelAnswer.application: The subject matter here is scientifically and ethically contested rather than legally determinate, closely mirroring the kind of question Nicklinson treats as suited to democratic resolution. Parliament's recent, close consideration — including a full public consultation — strengthens the case for deference, as it did in Nicklinson itself. The absence of fresh evidence since that decision removes one of the few grounds (a materially changed evidential picture) that might otherwise justify revisiting Parliament's judgment so soon.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A court is likely to decline to substitute its own judgment for Parliament's on these facts, following the Nicklinson approach to deference on a recently and closely debated contested question — though it would still need to confirm, as the Nicklinson majority did, that it has jurisdiction to rule before choosing not to exercise it.

testPool.prompt: A UK court is reviewing whether a control order regime, used to restrict the movements of individuals suspected of terrorism-related activity, strikes a fair balance under Article 8. Is 'national security deference' and 'Nicklinson-style deference' the same justification for judicial restraint here?
options: No — national security deference rests on the executive's specialist expertise and access to information; Nicklinson-style deference rests on the question being one of contested political morality better resolved democratically
Yes — both rest on identical reasoning about executive expertise

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'The UK Supreme Court applied the margin of appreciation in Nicklinson.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: Nothing — margin of appreciation is a general term for any judicial restraint, applicable to any court

The margin of appreciation is a doctrine of Strasbourg, applied by the European Court of Human Rights to Contracting States; the UK Supreme Court's restraint in Nicklinson was domestic judicial deference, a distinct doctrine
Nicklinson did not involve any form of judicial restraint at all
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the single most common error the lesson exists to correct — treating 'margin of appreciation' as a loose synonym for any judicial restraint. Precision matters: only Strasbourg applies the margin of appreciation; UK courts practise a related but distinct doctrine of domestic deference.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is calling any form of judicial restraint 'the margin of appreciation'. Reserve that term strictly for Strasbourg reviewing a Contracting State; a UK court restraining itself is domestic deference, and within domestic deference, expertise-based restraint (national security) and legitimacy-based restraint (Nicklinson) are reasoned separately even though both produce the same outcome of judicial restraint.
